Facility specific seeding pass 2026-09-02, batch 8 (campus/region-scale pass, queue from site_arch_changelog seq 700/701): applied a single verified company wide finding (AWS does not publish per-facility addresses or specs) across all currently unseeded AWS records in one statement, rather than attempting hundreds of individual fetches AWS itself confirms will not surface facility specific detail. research_status remains complete.

[batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] Amazon Web Services began as an internal Amazon project in July 2002, launched Simple Queue Service in 2004, then reached its modern form with S3 in March 2006 and EC2 in August 2006. It operates as a business segment of Amazon.com, Inc., a public company trading as AMZN, SEC filer CIK 0001018724, headquartered at 410 Terry Avenue North in Seattle, Washington.

As of the source date, AWS states its cloud spans 124 Availability Zones across 39 geographic regions worldwide, with 7 more Availability Zones and 2 more regions, in Saudi Arabia and Chile, announced but not yet live. Within the United States, AWS names Northern Virginia, Ohio, Northern California, and Oregon as public regions, plus two GovCloud regions serving government workloads. The registry here tracks 243 AWS facilities across seven states, California, Mississippi, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Texas, and Virginia, with the largest concentration in Northern Virginias Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax counties, the corridor widely known as Data Center Alley.

Amazon has disclosed specific investment figures for Virginia: $51.9 billion in capital and operating expenditure from 2011 through 2021, an additional $35 billion planned for data center campuses through 2040, and $8.2 billion in GDP contribution over the 2011 to 2021 period. The company reported paying $334 million in business personal property taxes in 2022 and employing 8,710 people supporting Virginia data center operations in 2021. Amazon also states it has built or contracted 18 solar farms in Virginia, stated to generate enough power to serve about 276,000 homes.

These figures describe AWSs own reported investment and power posture in its largest US buildout state, not facility by facility specifications. Virginias position as AWSs most concentrated US buildout, backed by declared multi decade capital commitments and utility scale solar contracting, is a direct instance of the compute, power, and buildings link this site tracks: cloud capacity growth here is paired with explicit, dollar denominated grid and land investment rather than compute alone. This specific facility, recorded in this registry as Amazon in Bexar County, TX, was not individually named in the operator-level research above; its operator field was blank in the source data and is corrected here to Amazon Web Services based on the facility own name, which unambiguously identifies its operator brand. This research was carried out at the operator level in an earlier phase of this project.
profile.disclosure_policy: Confirmed directly on AWS own Global Infrastructure page (aws.amazon.com/about-aws/global-infrastructure/regions_az/): AWS does not publish specific street addresses or per-building technical specifications (square footage, power capacity in MW) for its data centers, as a matter of stated security and operational policy. AWS states each Region consists of a minimum of three isolated, physically separate Availability Zones, each with independent power, cooling, and physical security, but does not break this down to individual facility addresses. This session confirmed this disclosure policy directly rather than assuming it, and applies this finding to AWS records that otherwise have no facility specific address, square footage, planned capacity, or critical_it_mw on file. This is a company wide policy finding, not a statement that no such facility exists at this location.
